verdict: Caution on new coal-mining and washery exposure in Asansol until ECL's rain-hit output and the mine-lift incident are quantified; lend only to washery and mining-services borrowers with contracted offtake and tight monthly stock-and-receivable controls.
title: Asansol coal mining & washeries: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Coal here is a volume-and-logistics business: rock is dug or washed, moved by road and rail, and paid for by offtake, not by the digging.** In Asansol the anchor is Eastern Coalfields' (ECL) mines and open-cast patches around Kenda, Kunustoria and Satgram, with private washeries and mining-services contractors feeding off that chain [2]. Cash is made on tonnes washed and dispatched; value sits in the washery yield and the transport leg, not in the seam itself.

## What has changed now
**Cyclonic rain has stopped production across several ECL areas, with losses feared in crores and no official tonnage estimate yet** [2]. Separately, miners were reported trapped in a Bengal mine lift on 26 October [3] — that is a safety and stoppage event, not a demand event. Peer results are strong: Bharat Coking Coal's October production rose 7% and offtake 11% [4], Coal India's Q2 profit rose 57% to INR 6,547 crore on revenue of INR 44,179 crore [7], and Q2FY27 production was 151 MT against a 158 MT target [6]. **Read this as: national offtake is healthy, local supply is disrupted — so the risk is at the borrower's mine gate, not at the customer's boiler.**

## Where the growth is
**Pursue washery operators and mining-services contractors with written offtake, not pure traders.** Washery capacity is being rebuilt across the sector — BCCL is commissioning washeries of 7.00 million tonnes per year and renovating Moonidih at 1.60 million tonnes per year [10] — and rated peers in washing and transport carry CRISIL BBB+/Stable [9][11]. Avoid single-mine contractors with no contract and no stock visibility; their cash stops the day the pit floods [2].

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the working-capital cycle, which is the real risk here: one rated peer pays suppliers in advance and recovers from customers in 45-60 days, funding the gap with bank borrowings** [8]. So when a proposal lands, check the receivable days against that 45-60 day band; if receivables stretch past it, ask for the customer-wise ageing and the offtake contract. Take monthly stock-and-yield statements, monthly dispatch and e-way bill data, and quarterly receivables ageing. Price the advance-payment leg into the limit, not the term loan.

## Early-warning signs
- **Rain or cyclone warnings for the Asansol belt (weekly, monsoon)** -> ask for pit dewatering status and expected restart date before any disbursement [2].
- **Any mine-safety or lift incident in the borrower's area (event-driven)** -> freeze fresh limits until the mine reopens [3].
- **Receivable days beyond 60 (monthly)** -> shift the borrower to cash-backed limits [8].
- **Washery yield or dispatch falling month-on-month (monthly)** -> cut the limit and ask for the offtake contract [10].

**Sources say little specific to Asansol borrowers themselves; the local items are ECL-level events, and the peer and rating data are national or other-company.** Collect from customer: borrower-wise production, washery yield, receivable ageing and contract terms.
watch: Cyclone or heavy-rain warning in the Asansol belt -> hold disbursement and get restart date [2]
Any lift or trapping incident in borrower's area -> freeze fresh limits until reopening [3]
Beyond 60 days -> move borrower to cash-backed limits [8]
Two consecutive months of decline -> cut limit, demand offtake contract [10]
Offtake falling below production -> check inventory build and price realisation [4][7]
